comes when the motion man reaches the quarterback, the defense knows when the snap is coming.**
A defense that times its own movement (a blitzer creeping up, a safety rotating) to the motion
man's arrival can move at the last instant without risking an offside penalty. Writing in
January 2024, Ben Solak of The Ringer pointed out that the two defenses then meeting in the AFC
Championship Game, Steve Spagnuolo's Chiefs and Mike Macdonald's Ravens, ranked first (Baltimore)
and sixth (Kansas City) in EPA per play allowed on snaps with motion, according to Next Gen
Stats, and that both made a habit of changing the whole picture as the motion triggered the
snap.[^ringer] The arms race moves to the last half-second.

### The "cheat motion" and the 2024 rule language

Motion at the snap reached the edge of the rulebook in 2023. Instead of sending a fast receiver
all the way across the formation, the Dolphins (and soon the 49ers and Rams) lined him up tight,
close to the tackle, and had him take a short, quick motion *outward*, toward his own sideline,
just before the snap, so that he could turn upfield at full speed the instant the ball moved: a
sprinter's rolling start. Kyle Shanahan called it a "little cheat motion" and admitted the 49ers
had copied it "in Week 2 after we saw it."[^cheat] Reporters noticed that Tyreek Hill sometimes
seemed to be turning upfield a fraction early, but he was never flagged for illegal motion all
season.

Was it legal? The rule said a player may not be moving *toward* the line at the snap, and the
officials judged that these motions were sideways at the moment the ball moved. For 2024 the
league added language to the false-start rule that was widely reported as aimed at the trick. An
eligible receiver who is **on the line** and moves backward or changes his stance (from a
two-point to a three-point stance, or back) now has to come to a **complete stop** before the
snap, or it's a false start; a player in the backfield who changes his stance doesn't have to
stop, as long as his movement isn't abrupt (a false start) or forward (illegal
motion).[^cheat2024]

Read that language next to the trick and you'll notice they don't quite meet. The cheat motion was
run by a receiver who had to be *off* the line to go in motion at all, moving sideways; the new sentence is about receivers *on* the
line stepping back or changing stance. League officials later told reporters exactly that: it was
a clarification, not a rule change, aimed at abrupt stance changes, and it did not outlaw
sideways motion that turns upfield at the snap. So the honest summary is that the cheat motion
itself survived. What the clarification ruled out was a neighbouring way to steal a start: a
receiver on the line rocking back or dropping into a stance at the last instant.

## The rulebook: NFL, college and Canada

You have the NFL's rule from the "You'll need" box: one backfield player, moving parallel to or
away from the line. Two details are worth adding.

First, a player who is *on the line* can't go in motion at all without first getting off it, and
that has real consequences. In Super Bowl LVII, when the Chiefs wanted to run their return-motion
play a second time, Patrick Mahomes signalled for Kadarius Toney to go in motion, but Toney was
lined up on the line of scrimmage and couldn't. Toney pointed across the field at Skyy Moore, who
was in the backfield, and Moore went instead; he scored the touchdown.[^wrongformation]

Second, the rule's purpose is the same as the one-second set's: **the offense may move before the
snap, but it may not get a running start at the line of scrimmage.** A sideways head start is
allowed; a forward one isn't.

| | NFL | NCAA (college) | CFL (Canada) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Players in motion at the snap | One | One | Any number of backfield players |
| Direction | Parallel to or away from the line | Not toward the opponent's goal line | Any direction, **including toward the line** |
| Who may move | A backfield player | A backfield player | Backfield players (not the quarterback) |

: Motion rules in three codes. American college rules match the NFL's in substance; Canadian rules are different in kind. {#tbl-motion-rules}

College football's rule is essentially the same as the NFL's: one player, not moving toward the
opponent's goal line at the snap, and a player who starts on the line has to become a back and come
to a complete stop before he can go in motion.[^ncaa]
The big outlier is Canadian football. In the CFL, every backfield player except the quarterback
may be in motion at the snap, in any direction, including **forward**.[^cfl] Canadian receivers
routinely hit the line of scrimmage at full speed as the ball is snapped (a "waggle"), which is
one reason the Canadian game, on a bigger field with twelve players a side, is so pass-heavy. If
you've wondered what would happen if the NFL allowed forward motion, the CFL is the experiment:
receivers that are nearly impossible to jam, and defenders who line up far off the ball to avoid
being run past.

## The motion boom, by the numbers

Motion is as old as the T formation (the Bears' man in motion in the 1940 championship game is
in [The Pre-Snap Phase](../01-foundations/01-05-the-pre-snap-phase.qmd)), and some coaches made
pre-snap movement a signature long before it was fashionable. Tom Landry's Cowboys of the 1960s
to 1980s famously had their offensive linemen stand up in unison and then drop back into their
stances while the backs shifted behind them, the "Landry shift," partly to hide the new backfield
alignment behind a wall of standing linemen.[^landry] But for most of NFL history motion was a
tool for particular plays, not a habit.

That changed in the late 2010s. Kyle Shanahan (49ers head coach from 2017) and Sean McVay (Rams
head coach from 2017) built offenses in which motion was part of almost every call, and as their
assistants became coordinators and head coaches around the league, the habit spread. By ESPN's
count, the 49ers used pre-snap motion on 69.1% of their plays from 2017 through 2021, the most in
the league, and on 76.9% in 2021 alone, while the league as a whole rose from 34.9% (2017) to
46.8% (2021).[^espnboom] PFF's longer shift-or-motion series, which
[The Pre-Snap Phase](../01-foundations/01-05-the-pre-snap-phase.qmd) quoted, shows the same climb
to a record **63.9%** in 2025, when every team except the Giants moved someone before at least
half of its snaps.[^pff]

Why the boom? Three reasons, each from earlier in this chapter. **Defenses started hiding their
coverage better**: Next Gen Stats measured two-high (split-safety) coverage on 32.9% of plays in 2018 and
42.0% in 2025, the highest since its tracking began,[^twohigh] and two-high shells are built to rotate,
so offenses needed a way to make them commit. **The head start became more valuable** as offenses
filled with very fast receivers. And **it worked visibly** for the offenses that did it most, so
it was copied.

Here is how the 32 teams moved, in FTN's charting.

```{python}
#| label: data-ftn
#| include: false
from gridiron.data import nfl, pbp

SEASONS = [2022, 2023, 2024, 2025]
ftn = nfl().load_ftn_charting(SEASONS).to_pandas()
PB_COLS = ["season", "season_type", "game_id", "play_id", "posteam", "play_type", "down", "epa", "pass"]
pb = pbp(SEASONS, columns=PB_COLS)
pb = pb[(pb.season_type == "REG") & pb.play_type.isin(["pass", "run"]) & pb.down.notna()]
mo = pb.merge(ftn[["nflverse_game_id", "nflverse_play_id", "is_motion"]],
              left_on=["game_id", "play_id"], right_on=["nflverse_game_id", "nflverse_play_id"], how="inner")
mo["is_motion"] = mo.is_motion.astype(float)
LEAGUE = mo.groupby("season").is_motion.mean()
TEAM = mo.groupby(["season", "posteam"]).is_motion.mean().unstack(0)
early = mo[mo.down.isin([1, 2])]
EPA = early.groupby(["season", "pass", "is_motion"]).epa.mean().unstack("is_motion")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-team-motion
#| fig-cap: "Share of each offense's plays with motion, NFL regular seasons 2022–2025, in FTN's charting (is_motion: motion before or at the snap; runs and passes only). Teams are sorted by 2025 and labelled with their standard abbreviations (LA is the Rams, LAC the Chargers); the teams this chapter discusses (MIA, SF, LA, KC, ATL, NYG) are in bold. Hollow circles are 2022, small grey ticks 2023 and 2024, filled circles 2025; the dashed lines are the league averages for 2022 and 2025. Almost every offense moved more in 2025 than in 2022. The 2023 Dolphins (79.4%) are the highest team-season in the four years. Only the Giants moved on fewer than 40% of their plays in 2025. Source: nflverse FTN charting and play-by-play; course calculation."
T = TEAM.sort_values(2025, ascending=True) * 100
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 6.0))
y = np.arange(len(T))
FOCUS = {"MIA", "SF", "LA", "KC", "ATL", "NYG"}
for yi, (team, row) in zip(y, T.iterrows()):
    ax.plot([row[2022], row[2025]], [yi, yi], color=style.GRID, lw=2.2, zorder=1, solid_capstyle="round")
    ax.plot([row[2023], row[2024]], [yi, yi], ls="", marker="|", ms=6, color=style.MUTED, zorder=2)
    ax.plot(row[2022], yi, ls="", marker="o", ms=5.2, mfc=style.SURFACE, mec=style.OFFENSE, mew=1.2, zorder=3)
    ax.plot(row[2025], yi, ls="", marker="o", ms=5.6, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, zorder=3)
for yr, txt in ((2022, "league 2022"), (2025, "league 2025")):
    v = LEAGUE[yr] * 100
    ax.axvline(v, color=style.INK_2, lw=0.8, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=0)
    ax.text(v + 0.6, len(T) - 0.2, f"{txt}\n{v:.1f}%", fontsize=6.8, color=style.INK_2, ha="left", va="bottom")
ax.set_yticks(y, T.index, fontsize=7)
for lab in ax.get_yticklabels():
    if lab.get_text() in FOCUS:
        lab.set_fontweight("bold")
        lab.set_color(style.INK)
mia = T.loc["MIA"]
ax.annotate(f"MIA 2023: {mia[2023]:.1f}%", xy=(mia[2023], y[list(T.index).index("MIA")]),
            xytext=(83.5, y[list(T.index).index("MIA")] - 3.2), fontsize=7, color=style.INK, ha="right",
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=style.MUTED, lw=0.7))
ax.set_xlim(15, 85)
ax.set_ylim(-0.8, len(T) + 1.6)
ax.set_xlabel("Plays with motion (%)", fontsize=8)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=7.5)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
hs = [Line2D([], [], ls="", marker="o", ms=5.2, mfc=style.SURFACE, mec=style.OFFENSE, mew=1.2, label="2022"),
      Line2D([], [], ls="", marker="|", ms=6, color=style.MUTED, label="2023, 2024"),
      Line2D([], [], ls="", marker="o", ms=5.6, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, label="2025")]
ax.legend(handles=hs, fontsize=7.2, loc="lower right", ncol=3)
plt.show()
```

The league average rose from about 38% to 55% in four seasons in FTN's data, and the spread
between teams is wide: the Dolphins, 49ers, Rams and Falcons sat near the top for most of the
period, while the Giants were the one 2025 offense below 40%. Notice how some teams jumped as soon
as they changed play-callers: the Saints went from about 30% to 51% in 2024, Klint Kubiak's first
season as their offensive coordinator, and the Eagles from 23% to 44% in Kellen Moore's. Motion is a *coaching* choice more than a personnel one;
it follows the play-caller.

### Why the motion numbers disagree

You will see wildly different "motion rates" quoted for the same season: 22%, 55%, 64%. They are
not contradictions. They are different measurements.

```{python}
#| label: fig-motion-series
#| fig-cap: "Three published motion series, each on its own panel because they measure different things. PFF counts any pre-snap shift or motion (2014–2025). FTN's is_motion counts plays with motion before or at the snap, charted by FTN (2022–2025, course calculation from nflverse). ESPN Analytics counts a player in motion at the moment of the snap; only two league-average points are published in the sources used here (2017 and 2023), drawn as hollow, unconnected points because they come from press reports, not a data file. All three rise; the levels differ because the definitions do. Never plot them on one axis as if they were one series."
SERIES = [
    ("PFF: shift or motion", {2014: 37.6, 2016: 38.4, 2018: 43.0, 2019: 46.8, 2020: 50.0, 2021: 51.8, 2022: 55.4,
                                   2023: 56.4, 2024: 61.5, 2025: 63.9}, True),
    ("FTN: motion by the snap", {yr: LEAGUE[yr] * 100 for yr in SEASONS}, True),
    ("ESPN: motion at the snap", {2017: 4.0, 2023: 22.0}, False),
]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(6.5, 2.55), sharey=True)
for ax, (ttl, ser, solid) in zip(axes, SERIES):
    xs, ys = list(ser), list(ser.values())
    if solid:
        ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.8, marker="o", ms=3.4)
    else:
        ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.OFFENSE, ls="", marker="o", ms=4.8, mfc=style.SURFACE, mew=1.3)
    for x_, y_ in ((xs[0], ys[0]), (xs[-1], ys[-1])):
        ax.text(x_, y_ + 3.2, f"{y_:.0f}%" if solid else f"~{y_:.0f}%", fontsize=7, ha="center", color=style.INK)
    ax.set_title(ttl, fontsize=7.8, loc="left")
    ax.set_xlim(2013.3, 2025.9)
    ax.set_xticks([2014, 2018, 2022, 2025])
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=6.8)
    ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
axes[0].set_ylim(0, 75)
axes[0].set_ylabel("Share of plays (%)", fontsize=7.5)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

Four things make the numbers differ, and each is worth knowing before you quote one:

1. **What counts as movement.** PFF counts shifts *and* motion. FTN's `is_motion` flag means
   "motion occurred on the play before or at the time of the snap." ESPN's headline series counts
   only a player *still moving* at the snap, a much smaller set. Next Gen Stats publishes yet
   another pair, total pre-snap motion and motion at the snap: Atlanta's 70.1% and 60.8% in
   2025, quoted above.
2. **Who or what does the charting.** PFF and FTN use human charters watching video; Next Gen
   Stats uses the player-tracking chips. A human charter and a tracking threshold can disagree
   about whether a receiver's two-step shuffle "counts."
3. **Which plays are in the denominator.** All snaps, or only runs and passes? Are kneel-downs,
   spikes and penalty-only plays included? Playoffs? These shift a rate by a point or two.
4. **Which seasons exist.** FTN's charting in nflverse starts in 2022, ESPN's motion-at-the-snap
   series in 2017, PFF's runs back further.

The rule this book follows: **every motion number carries its source, and two sources never
share an axis.** When you compare teams or seasons, compare them inside one series.

### Does motion work?

The honest answer is "yes, but not in the way a simple average suggests." In FTN's data, plays
with motion and plays without it look surprisingly alike. On first and second downs in 2025,
passes with motion averaged about +0.10
[EPA](../01-foundations/01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd) per play against +0.06
without, and runs about −0.05 against −0.08; in 2024 the two were nearly identical, and in 2022
passes *without* motion did better.[^epa] Teams that motion more did have slightly better
offenses in each of the four seasons, but the relationship is loose.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"Motion plays gain more, so offenses should motion on every play." The averages above don't show
that, and even if they did, the comparison wouldn't prove it. Offenses *choose* when to motion:
some save it for their best-designed plays, some motion on almost everything, and defenses adjust
to teams that motion a lot. The plays with and without motion aren't a controlled experiment.
Other comparisons find more: ESPN's numbers for 2017–2023, as reported by The Ringer in 2024, had
runs with motion *at the snap* gaining about 0.11 EPA per play more than runs with no motion, and
dropbacks about 0.08 more.[^ringer2] That is a simple with-and-without comparison too, though, so
it carries the same caution.
Part of motion's value is also invisible in its own plays: a motion that always meant "run" would
be a [tell](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd), so offenses use the same
motions on different plays to keep the defense from reading them. Measuring that kind of value is
part of [Tendencies: PROE, Personnel, Motion, and Coverage](../13-analytics-and-data/13-04-tendencies-proe-and-charting.qmd).
:::

## Film room

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Miami Dolphins 2023, motion at the snap"}
No offense in the tracking era moved like Mike McDaniel's 2023 Dolphins. In FTN's charting they
used motion on 79.4% of their runs and passes, the highest team-season from 2022 to 2025; ESPN had
them with a player in motion at the snap on 59% of plays early that season, a record. They
scored 70 points against Denver in Week 3, and Tyreek Hill led the NFL with 1,799 receiving
yards.[^hill]

What to notice when you watch the film: the motion is short and *timed*. Hill or Jaylen Waddle
moves a few yards, sometimes in toward the formation, sometimes out toward the sideline (the
"cheat" version), and the ball is snapped as he gets going. The defense rarely gets a clean look
at its own assignment, and Hill starts every route already running. Then watch the defenses that
slowed Miami down. The Chiefs, who beat the Dolphins twice that season (in Frankfurt in November
and in the wild-card round), mostly refused to chase: in the November game they played zone on a
season-high 61% of Miami's dropbacks, by ESPN's count, with Steve Spagnuolo's instruction to keep "22 eyeballs" on Hill, and L'Jarius Sneed matched Hill when they
did play man.[^kcmia] McDaniel was let go by Miami in January 2026 and is the Chargers'
offensive coordinator for the 2026 season.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Kansas City Chiefs, Super Bowl LVII (February 12, 2023)"}
Two of the most famous motion plays of the decade came less than three minutes of game clock apart. In the fourth quarter
against the Eagles, Kansas City ran a play its coaches call "Corn Dog": a receiver motions in
toward the formation, then turns and runs back toward the sideline at the snap, a return motion
built to beat man coverage. Kadarius Toney caught a 5-yard touchdown on it with 12:04 left to give
the Chiefs the lead, and Skyy Moore scored from 4 yards on a mirrored version at 9:22. Both times
the Eagles were in man coverage, the defender went with the first move, and the receiver was alone
when he turned around. Kansas City won 38–35. A year later in Super Bowl LVIII the Chiefs ran a
renamed relative of the play for Mecole Hardman's winning touchdown in overtime.[^corndog]

What to notice: the motion does *two* jobs on one play. First it asks the question (did the
defender follow?), and then it attacks the answer (the defender who followed is moving the wrong
way). Andy Reid's offense has used motion that way for years, including orbit motion that loops a
receiver behind the quarterback and out to the flat, pulling defenders with him while the real
target comes open elsewhere.[^orbitkc]
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: San Francisco 49ers 2021, Deebo Samuel"}
In 2021 the 49ers motioned on 76.9% of their plays, the most in the league by ESPN's count.
Much of it went through Deebo Samuel, a wide receiver who spent part of the season lining up and
motioning into the backfield. Motion let Shanahan move Samuel from receiver to ball carrier and
back again before the snap, so the defense never knew which position it was defending. He caught
passes for 1,405 yards and ran for 365 more, with eight rushing touchdowns.[^deebo]

What to notice: the motion *creates the matchup*. When Samuel motioned from a receiver spot into the
backfield, the defender assigned to him in man coverage had to follow him into the box, where a
cornerback or safety is suddenly playing run defense against a 215-pound receiver with a head start.
Against zone, the defense now faced a backfield with two ball carriers in it, one of them very fast,
and had to respect both.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Los Angeles Rams 2017–2025, the same look, different plays"}
McVay's Rams were not the league's most frequent motion team in his first seasons (ESPN had them
eighth from 2017 to 2021), but they made the jet motion famous, and by 2024 FTN charted
them with motion on 76.7% of their plays, the highest in the league that season. The Rams' trademark
is pairing: over a game, the same jet look comes before an outside-zone run, a jet sweep and a
play-action pass, so the motion tells the defense nothing about the play. What to notice: the
play was called in the huddle, so the defense's reaction doesn't change *this* play; it tells you
which one should work. Watch the linebackers when the jet man crosses the quarterback. If they
jump toward him, the run the other way should hit; if they stay home, expect the Rams to give it
to the jet man on a later snap.
:::

## The checklist so far

Part 2 ends here, and with it the first version of the card you will carry through the rest of
the book. Each line is a question you can answer before the snap, in the order the answers
become visible on a broadcast (the order [Personnel](02-01-personnel-groupings.qmd) introduced):
the situation first, then who is on the field, then where they line up, then what the motion
draws out of the defense, then the box and the safeties.

```{python}
#| label: fig-checklist
#| fig-cap: "The watching checklist after Part 2. Line 1 comes from Part 1; lines 2 to 6 are the pre-snap reads Part 2 taught, in the order they become visible during a snap; line 7 is the habit from How to Watch a Broadcast. The motion line is this chapter's. The card grows after Parts 4, 6 and 7, and becomes the master checklist of the capstone."
items = [
    ("BEFORE THE SNAP", None, None, False),
    ("1", "Situation: down, distance, field zone, clock and score", "Part 1", False),
    ("2", "Personnel: who is on the field for each side (two digits for the offense; base, nickel or dime)",
     "02-01, 02-05", True),
    ("3", "Formation and strength: under center or gun, 2x2 or 3x1, where is the tight end?", "02-02 to 02-04", True),
    ("4", "Motion: does a defender travel (man)? Do they bump (zone, unless the slid defenders end up tight "
          "on one man: an exchange)? Does a safety spin (one-high)? Is the ball snapped while he's still moving?",
     "02-06", True),
    ("5", "Box count: blockers against defenders near the line (light box: run; loaded box: pass)", "02-05", True),
    ("6", "Shell: one-high or two-high? Did the motion change it?", "02-05, 02-06", True),
    ("AFTER THE PLAY", None, None, False),
    ("7", "Log it: your run/pass and man/zone calls against what happened", "01-06, 02-06", False),
]
rows = []
for num, text, where, new in items:
    if text is None:
        rows.append(("head", num, 1))
    else:
        lines_ = textwrap.wrap(text, 62)
        rows.append(("item", (num, lines_, where, new), len(lines_)))
n_lines = sum(h for _, _, h in rows) + 4
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 0.24 * n_lines))
ax.set_xlim(0, 100); ax.set_ylim(0, n_lines); ax.axis("off")
ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((0.8, 0.3), 98.4, n_lines - 0.6, boxstyle="round,pad=0.2,rounding_size=0.8",
                            fc=style.SURFACE, ec=style.BASELINE, lw=1.2))
ax.text(3, n_lines - 1.3, "Watching checklist · after Part 2", fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK,
        va="center")
ax.text(97, n_lines - 1.3, "new in Part 2", fontsize=8, color=style.INK_2, ha="right", va="center",
        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.3", fc=style.OFFENSE_TINT, ec="none"))
yy = n_lines - 2.8
for kind, payload, h in rows:
    if kind == "head":
        ax.text(3, yy, payload, fontsize=8, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK_2, va="center")
        yy -= 1.0
        continue
    num, lines_, where, new = payload
    top, bottom = yy + 0.45, yy - (h - 1) - 0.45
    if new:
        ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((2.2, bottom), 95.6, top - bottom, boxstyle="round,pad=0.05,rounding_size=0.4",
                                    fc=style.OFFENSE_TINT, ec="none"))
    ax.text(5.5, yy, num, fontsize=8.5, fontweight="bold", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, va="center", ha="center")
    for j, ln in enumerate(lines_):
        ax.text(9.0, yy - j, ln, fontsize=8, color=style.INK, va="center")
    ax.text(97, yy, where, fontsize=7, color=style.INK_2, va="center", ha="right")
    yy -= h + 0.15
plt.show()
```

Two habits make the card work. **Say each answer out loud, or write it down, before the snap.**
A guess you didn't commit to can't teach you anything. And **read the lines in order.** The motion
line comes after the formation line because you can't interpret a defender's reaction until you
know what the motion did to the formation; the shell line comes last because the motion may have
changed it.

## Watch for it on Sunday

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it: follow the motion"}
For one quarter, every time an offensive player moves before the snap, do four things.

- **Name it.** Jet, orbit, return, zoom, glide, short, a trade, a shift? If you aren't sure, describe
  the path ("across, in front of the quarterback").
- **Watch who follows.** Pick up the defender who was across from the motion man *before* he moved.
  Did that defender travel across (T), did the defenders bump over (B), did a safety spin (S)? Write
  the letters. If it was a bump, look at where the slid defender stopped: tight on one man (an
  exchange, so man) or in a space between receivers (zone)?
- **Call it.** Man or zone? One-high or two-high at the snap? Write your call before the ball is
  snapped.
- **Note the timing.** Was the ball snapped while he was still moving (motion at the snap), or did he
  set first?

Then check your calls on the replay, or better, on the All-22 film, which shows the whole secondary.
Add a column for it in your prediction log from
[How to Watch a Broadcast](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd). After a few games
you'll notice two things: travellers are rarer than you expect (many man defenses
[exchange](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-exchange-man-coverage-on-motion) instead), and your
calls get better when the motion is at the snap.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 1: who went with him?"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-travel
#| fig-cap: "Second-and-7. Before the motion the defense shows two deep safeties. Then H, in the left slot, motions across the formation, and the nickel back (NB, ringed) runs with him the whole way. As he does, the safety on the right (SS) comes down to about 8 yards in the middle of the field and the safety on the left (FS) slides over to the deep middle. Dashed paths are pre-snap movement. The ball is snapped as H reaches the right side."
off = gun_2x2_spread()
dfn = front4(sde=5.0) + [
    D("LCB", "CB", 5.5, -15.5, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 5.5, 15.5, "CB"), D("NB", "NB", 4.8, -9.5, "NB"),
    D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 1.5, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.5, "W"), D("SS", "SS", 13.0, 8.5, "SS"),
    D("FS", "FS", 13.0, -8.5, "FS")]
q = Play(off, dfn, los=45, to_go=7)
q.motion("H", pts=[(-1.0, 5.0), (-1.3, 14.0), (-0.5, 20.0), (-0.5, 21.0)])
q.motion("NB", pts=[(0.2, 4.0), (0.3, 12.0), (0.2, 20.0), (0.1, 21.5)])
dashed_motion(q, "SS", (9.2, -0.5))
dashed_motion(q, "FS", (14.0, -0.5))
q.highlight("NB", color=style.THIRD)
fld = q.draw(lateral=(-20.5, 20.5), window=(-7.5, 17.5), title=False)
no_numbers(fld.ax)
P = P_of(fld, q)
callout(fld.ax, P, "snap as H\narrives", (-5.6, 15.0), (-2.2, 12.0), fs=7.2, ec=style.THIRD)
plt.show()
```

**Man or zone? How many deep safeties? And what does the offense like about the picture?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Man coverage, with one deep safety: Cover 1, almost certainly.** Two things happened at once.
The nickel back travelled with H all the way across the formation, which a zone defender has no
reason to do: that says man. And the safeties spun: the two-high picture turned into one safety in
the deep middle and one at 8 yards in the middle of the field, a classic spot for a "robber" who
lurks underneath looking for crossing routes (see
[Man Coverage](../06-pass-coverage/06-02-man-coverage.qmd)). Notice that this spin didn't drop the
safety out toward the motion side; it dropped him into the middle. Spins vary in where the down
safety lands; the part that matters for your call is that two deep became one. Travel plus spin is
the signature of man coverage disguised as two-high before the motion.

What the offense likes: H's defender is now **behind and inside** a receiver who is moving toward
the sideline at full speed. A flat route, a wheel up the sideline, or a quick throw to H the instant
the ball is snapped all start as races the nickel back is losing. On the other side, X is alone
with his corner, and with the single deep safety in the middle there is no help over the top on the
outside. Man coverage also means most defenders have their backs turned to the quarterback, so a
quarterback who can run has open grass if the routes clear out the middle.

The caution: a robber in the middle is there precisely to jump the crossing routes that beat man
coverage, so throwing a shallow cross into him is the mistake the defense is hoping for.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 2: the third-quarter jet"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-jet
#| fig-cap: "Third quarter, first-and-10. Six times in the first half the offense ran this exact jet motion by Z and handed the ball to the running back going the other way. This time, as Z starts across, the defensive end on the side he is heading to (E, ringed) shifts his alignment about a yard and a half inside, and the two linebackers (ringed) stay on their spots. The nickel (NB) is over H, the left corner (CB) 7 yards off X, and the safeties 13 yards deep, one on each side. Z is 2 yards from the quarterback when the ball is snapped."
off = gun_2x1_te()
dfn = front4() + [
    D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -15.5, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 15.5, "CB"), D("NB", "NB", 5.5, -10.0, "NB"),
    D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 1.2, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.5, "W"),
    D("FS", "FS", 13.0, -9.0, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 13.0, 9.0, "SS")]
q = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=10)
q.motion("Z", pts=[(-0.9, -5.0), (-1.4, -10.0), (-1.5, -12.6)])
dashed_motion(q, "WDE", (1.0, -3.4))
q.highlight("MIKE", "WILL", "WDE", color=style.THIRD)
fld = q.draw(lateral=(-20.5, 20.5), window=(-7.5, 15.5), title=False)
no_numbers(fld.ax)
P = P_of(fld, q)
callout(fld.ax, P, "linebackers:\nsame spots", (9.5, -6.5), (5.0, -1.6), ec=style.THIRD)
callout(fld.ax, P, "end: shifts\ninside", (-4.5, -11.0), (0.7, -3.9), ec=style.THIRD)
plt.show()
```

**What should the offense call here, and why does it work only because of the first half?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Give the ball to Z: the jet sweep itself.** The defense has learned that the jet is a fake and
the run is coming the other way, so it has stopped spending players on the jet. The linebackers
stay home to play the running back, and the end on Z's side has pinched inside to close the
back's path, a pre-snap tell that he means to crash. Now count the jet side. H blocks the nickel,
who is the defender responsible for turning the play back inside (the force player); X stalks the
corner; and the only unblocked defender left on that side is the safety 13 yards deep, too far
away to get to the edge before Z does. Z already has a head start; with the end inside and nobody
flowing with him, he gets the corner.

That is the logic of jet motion as a *constraint*: the fake is only worth something if the real
thing is a threat. Run the inside handoff enough and the defense ignores the jet; run the jet when
it does. Offenses build their game plans around exactly this pairing (more in
[Perimeter Runs and Misdirection](../03-the-run-game/03-05-perimeter-and-misdirection.qmd) and
[Constraint Theory and Sequencing](../08-the-chess-match/08-02-constraint-theory-and-sequencing.qmd)).
The defense's counter is to keep at least one player honest on the jet side: a safety who spins
toward the motion, as in the zone animation earlier, would have been waiting.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 3: nobody went with him"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-empty
#| fig-cap: "Third-and-6. The running back (R) motions out of the backfield and sets wide on the right, between Y and Z, leaving the backfield empty. Nobody follows him across. The strong safety (SS, ringed), who was 7 yards deep over Y, slides out and stops about 3 yards in front of the back, just inside him. The Mike linebacker (M, ringed) slides out of the box and stops about 4 yards in front of Y, just inside him. One deep safety (FS) stays in the middle. Dashed paths are pre-snap movement; dashed outlines are where the two defenders started."
RB_SET, SS_SET, M_SET = (-1.5, 12.3), (1.6, 11.6), (3.0, 8.2)
off = [q.moved(d=RB_SET[0], w=RB_SET[1]) if q.key == "RB" else q for q in gun_2x2_spread()]
dfn = front4(sde=5.0) + [
    D("LCB", "CB", 7.5, -15.5, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.5, 15.5, "CB"), D("NB", "NB", 5.0, -9.5, "NB"),
    D("SS", "SS", *SS_SET, "SS"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", *M_SET, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -3.0, "W"),
    D("FS", "FS", 13.5, 0.0, "FS")]
q = Play(off, dfn, los=45, to_go=6)
q.highlight("SS", "MIKE", color=style.THIRD)
fld = q.draw(lateral=(-20.5, 20.5), window=(-7.5, 16.5), title=False)
no_numbers(fld.ax)
P = P_of(fld, q)
ghost_marker(fld.ax, *P(-5.0, -1.6), "R", fld.pts_per_yard(), side="off")
mpath(fld.ax, P, [(-5.0, -1.6), (-4.6, 2.4), (-3.2, 8.0), (-2.2, 11.0), (-1.7, 11.7)])
for start, end, lab in (((7.5, 8.0), SS_SET, "SS"), ((4.5, 0.8), M_SET, "M")):
    ghost_marker(fld.ax, *P(*start), lab, fld.pts_per_yard())
    dpath(fld.ax, P, start, end)
callout(fld.ax, P, "box: 5 defenders", (10.0, -7.0), (4.6, -3.0))
plt.show()
```

**The running-back test said that in man coverage a linebacker walks out with the back. Nobody
did. Is this zone? Look at where the two defenders who slid ended up.**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Probably still man coverage, Cover 1, played with an exchange.** Nobody travelled, so the
first-glance read is zone, and that is exactly what the defense wants you to think. But look at
where the slid defenders stopped. The strong safety is three yards in front of the back and just
inside him, squared up on one man. The Mike is four yards in front of Y and just inside him, also
squared up on one man. Zone defenders on that side would have stopped at area depth, five to
seven yards, *between* Y and the back, waiting for whoever came into their space. Two defenders
each pairing up with one receiver is man coverage; the defense simply passed the back to the
safety and pushed the Mike out onto Y instead of sending the Mike across with the back.

So the running-back test needs one refinement: the tell isn't "the Mike walks out", it's "**a
box defender** leaves to take a receiver". Here one did, just not the one you were watching. The
box is down to five defenders (four linemen and the Will) against five blockers, with one deep
safety behind them.

What the offense likes: a linebacker in man coverage on Y in open space, and a safety on a
running back, are both matchups the offense created on purpose; a quick option route by Y or an
out by the back is often the first read. With every defender's back turned and the middle
thinned, a quarterback scramble is open on third-and-6. The caution: an empty backfield leaves no
back to pick up an extra rusher, so if the Will or the nickel blitzes, the ball has to come out
quickly (see [Pass Protection](../04-the-passing-game/04-02-pass-protection.qmd)). And if at the
snap the safety and the Mike *drop* instead of turning to run with their men, the read was wrong:
log it, and look for what you missed.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- **Motion is never decoration.** Every motion does at least one of five jobs: it asks *man or
  zone?*, changes the strength and the numbers (receivers or blockers), gives a running start,
  creates leverage, or stresses the defense's communication. A shift moves several players and
  rebuilds the formation, but it costs a one-second freeze and gives nobody a running start.
- **Learn the shapes, not just the names.** Jet, fly and orbit cross the formation (in front of,
  behind, and looping behind the quarterback); rocket sprints a back to the edge; return goes and
  comes back; zoom crosses and sets; glide comes in and is still moving at the snap, short motion
  comes in and sets; a trade or a shift to bunch rebuilds the formation. Names vary by playbook.
- **Read the answer, then check it.** A defender who **travels** suggests man; defenders who
  **bump** suggest zone; safeties who **spin** turn two-high into one-high. But a man defense can
  **exchange**, sliding over just like a zone, so look at where the slid defenders stop: tight on
  one receiver means man, sitting in a space between receivers means zone. Pattern-matching zones
  can follow, and safeties can spin back. This read is line 4 of the checklist so far: situation →
  personnel → formation and strength → the motion response → box → shell, then log it.
- **The later the motion, the more it's worth.** Motion at the snap gives a running start worth
  about three yards in the first second (in the direction of the motion) and leaves the defense no
  time to disguise, but it also leaves the quarterback no time to check the play. NFL use of it
  rose from about 4% of plays in 2017 to over 20% by 2023 (ESPN).
- **The rules shape the motion.** American rules allow one backfield player moving sideways or
  back at the snap; Canadian rules let backs move forward. The 2024 NFL language on receivers who
  change stance on the line was a clarification that left the sideways "cheat motion" legal.
- **Motion numbers depend on the source.** PFF (any shift or motion: 63.9% in 2025), FTN (motion
  before or at the snap: 55.1%), ESPN and Next Gen Stats (motion at the snap) all measure different
  things. Quote one source at a time.

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper"}
- **Big Data Bowl 2025** was built around exactly this chapter's question: what pre-snap movement
  reveals about the play. Its files include, for every player on every play from the first nine
  weeks of 2022, flags for whether he was in motion at the snap and whether he shifted or went in
  motion after the line set. Once you have the files, this is how you'd start:

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (Big Data Bowl 2025: motion flags and coverage)"
import pandas as pd
from gridiron import bdb, show_animation

pp = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/player_play.csv")      # one row per player per play
plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")         # one row per play, with PFF's coverage labels
FLAGS = ["inMotionAtBallSnap", "motionSinceLineset", "shiftSinceLineset"]
KEYS = ["gameId", "playId"]
flags = pp.groupby(KEYS)[FLAGS].max().reset_index()          # True if any player did it
flags = flags.merge(plays[KEYS + ["possessionTeam", "pff_manZone"]], on=KEYS)
print(flags[FLAGS].mean())                                   # share of plays with each
print(pd.crosstab(flags.inMotionAtBallSnap, flags.pff_manZone, normalize="index"))

# animate one play with motion at the snap, drawn like this chapter's diagrams
trk = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb/tracking_week_1.csv")
wk1 = flags[flags.gameId.isin(trk.gameId.unique())]          # only plays in the week-1 file just loaded
g, pl = wk1.loc[wk1.inMotionAtBallSnap == True, KEYS].iloc[0]
show_animation(bdb.prepare(trk, plays, game_id=g, play_id=pl))
```

- Ben Solak's January 2024 piece in *The Ringer* on how the Chiefs' and Ravens' defenses answered
  motion, and Nick Wagoner and Lindsey Thiry's 2022 ESPN piece on Shanahan's and McVay's motion
  habits (both linked in the notes).
- Chris B. Brown, *The Art of Smart Football* (2015), for the older roots of motion and shifts in
  offensive design.
:::

[^espn2022]: Nick Wagoner and Lindsey Thiry, "49ers' Kyle Shanahan and Rams' Sean McVay always thinking pre-snap motion," ESPN (Jan. 29, 2022): 49ers 69.1% pre-snap motion 2017–2021 (first), Rams 46.3% (eighth); 2021: 49ers 76.9% (first), Rams 47.4%; league 34.9% (2017) to 46.8% (2021); quotes from Shanahan and McVay: https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/32598845/

[^names]: Definitions of jet, orbit and return motion as coaches teach them: Ryan Swingle, "Install Motion Into Your Offense (Coaching Guide)," Viqtory Sports (updated Jan. 27, 2026): https://www.viqtorysports.com/pre-snap-movement-in-the-offense/ . The guide notes that jet motion is "also known as the 'Fly' motion in some terminology, especially in the Wing-T." Glide, zoom and short (rip/liz) motion have no single published standard; the meanings used here are this book's convention, and individual playbooks differ.

[^rocket]: In the flexbone rocket toss the backside A-back (slotback) leaves in fast motion about a second before the snap ("If the cadence is Down, Ready, Set-hut, the Backside A-back leaves after the Down") and the quarterback pitches to him at the edge: "Flexbone Triple Option Offense Coaching: Drilling the Rocket Toss with the Skill Positions," Triple Option Football (Oct. 13, 2013): https://tripleoptionfootball.com/?p=1496 . The use of "rocket" for a running back's fast motion out of a shotgun backfield is playbook dialect, not a standard.

[^espnsnap]: ESPN Analytics (Seth Walder), as reported by Ben Solak, *The Ringer* (Jan. 25, 2024): an average NFL team snapped the ball with a player in motion on 4% of plays in 2017 and 22% in 2023: https://www.theringer.com/nfl/2024/1/25/24050457/kansas-city-chiefs-baltimore-ravens-afc-championship-steve-spagnuolo-mike-macdonald-defense-motion . (ESPN's league figures for 2024 and 2025 appear only second-hand, with conflicting numbers, so this book does not quote them.)

FTN figure (79.4% of 2023 regular-season runs and passes with `is_motion`) is a course calculation from nflverse.

[^cheat]: John Breech, "NFL shuts down rulebook loophole that Dolphins, 49ers and Rams were exploiting during 2023 season," CBS Sports (Aug. 1, 2024), including Shanahan's "The [Dolphins] did that in Week 1 with a little cheat motion. We did it in Week 2 after we saw it": https://www.cbssports.com/nfl/news/nfl-shuts-down-rulebook-loophole-that-dolphins-49ers-and-rams-were-exploiting-during-2023-season ; on the alignment (receivers set close to the tackle, sprinting toward the near sideline just before the snap), *San Francisco Chronicle* (Sept. 29, 2023): https://preview-prod.w.sfchronicle.com/sports/49ers/article/ex-49er-coordinator-s-cheat-motion-brings-bit-18394475.php ; Alain Poupart, *Sports Illustrated* (All Dolphins, Aug. 1, 2024): "Hill never was called for an illegal forward motion penalty last season": https://www.si.com/nfl/dolphins/tyreek-and-the-commotion-about-the-cheat-motion-01j47qrysqyj

[^cheat2024]: NFL rule language added for 2024, now Rule 7, Section 4, Article 2, Item 2 (False Start, Eligible Receiver) of the 2026 rulebook (https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/): "If an eligible receiver who is on the line of scrimmage moves backward or changes his stance (two point to three point or conversely) and does not come to a complete stop before the snap, it is a false start. Any eligible backfield player who changes his stance does not have to come to a complete stop prior to the snap, as long as his actions are not abrupt (false start) or forward (illegal motion)." That NFL officials described it as a clarification, not a rule change, aimed at sudden stance changes rather than lateral jet motion: Alain Poupart, "Clarity on the Cheat Motion Commotion," *Sports Illustrated* (All Dolphins, Aug. 14, 2024): https://www.si.com/nfl/dolphins/news/clarity-on-the-cheat-motion-commotion-01j591m7stgc

[^wrongformation]: "Chiefs lined up in wrong formation on pivotal Super Bowl play and Patrick Mahomes still managed to throw a TD," John Breech, CBS Sports (Feb. 16, 2023): Toney "was lined up on the line of scrimmage, so he couldn't move," pointed across to Moore, and Mahomes sent Moore in motion instead: https://www.cbssports.com/nfl/news/chiefs-lined-up-in-wrong-formation-on-pivotal-super-bowl-play-and-patrick-mahomes-still-managed-to-throw-a-td

[^ncaa]: NCAA, *Football Rules and Interpretations*, Rule 7-1-4-b: "One back may be in motion, but he may not be moving toward his opponent's goal line"; "The player who goes in motion may not start from the line of scrimmage unless he first becomes a back and comes to a complete stop"; text as reproduced in the BAFA rulebook, which adopts the NCAA code: https://rules.bafra.info/rulebook/bafa2020/7.html ; NCAA rules: https://www.ncaapublications.com/c-4-rules.aspx ; summary of the NFL/NCAA/high-school rule (one player, not moving toward the line) in "Motion (gridiron football)," *Wikipedia*: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motion_(gridiron_football)

[^cfl]: CFL rulebook (2025), Rule 4: the motion limits apply to *line* players, who must be motionless for one second before the snap and "No player of Team A, who is a Line Player, shall be moving towards the opponent's Goal Line when the ball is put in play" (Section 5, Article 4); the quarterback's movements are restricted separately (Section 2, Article 2); no article limits the other backs, who must only be behind the line at the snap (Section 2, Article 3). Rulebook text via CFLdb: https://cfldb.ca/rulebook/scrimmage/player-restrictions/ and https://cfldb.ca/rulebook/scrimmage/method-of-scrimmage/ ; official rules: https://www.cfl.ca/rules-and-regulations/ ; summary in "Motion (gridiron football)," *Wikipedia*: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motion_(gridiron_football)

[^landry]: "ITP Glossary: Landry Shift," Integrated Scouting Academy: https://scoutingacademy.com/itp-glossary-landry-shift/ (all linemen but the center rise from a three-point stance to a two-point stance and back down before the snap, while the backs shift behind them, "making it more difficult to see the new alignment of the backs"; used in the 1960s, '70s and '80s); "Cowboys' homage to Landry was a player decision," DallasCowboys.com (2014), with Jason Garrett's description ("when Roger said 'Shift,' … the backs would shift behind him"): https://www.dallascowboys.com/news/cowboys-homage-to-landry-was-a-player-decision-358106

[^twohigh]: Next Gen Stats via NFL.com, "The coverage that turned the Seahawks into Super Bowl winners and is taking the NFL by storm": split-safety coverage 32.9% (2018), 42.0% (2025): https://www.nfl.com/news/the-coverage-that-turned-the-seahawks-into-super-bowl-winners-and-is-taking-the-nfl-by-storm

Correlation between a team's motion rate and its EPA per play (all downs): 0.24 (2022), 0.43 (2023), 0.23 (2024), 0.24 (2025).
